answer.answer: I don’t have enough operating conditions to give a meaningful battery fast-charging protocol. The retrieved literature shows that fast-charge methods are highly cell- and condition-specific, with reported protocols depending on chemistry, form factor, temperature, and state-of-charge window. For example, one paper reports a stepwise protocol for a constrained pouch Li-ion/graphite cell at 25 °C that charged 0% to 85% SoC in 26.8 min with >95% SoH after 100 cycles, while another reports a 4C-based protocol for an LFP high-power cylindrical cell with a 5 min CV limit and a manufacturer-current margin to reduce overheating. A simulation study also suggests voltage-ramping or multiple-CCCV approaches can reduce lithium plating risk, but explicitly says experimental validation was ongoing. Because your known operating conditions are empty, I can’t responsibly recommend a specific protocol or limits.

evidence.finding: Stepwise fast-charge protocol for a constrained pouch Li-ion/graphite cell at 25 °C charged 0% to 85% SoC in 26.8 min; after 100 cycles, SoH remained over 95% with no abnormalities reported.

For an LFP high-power cylindrical cell, a 4C fast-charge stage was used near the manufacturer-recommended maximum current with a 12% security margin; CV charging was limited to 5 min to reduce aging at high SoC.
Simulation-only study proposed voltage-ramping and multiple-CCCV protocols to improve fast charging without lithium plating; authors stated experimental validation was ongoing.

Results and Discussion
The shown fast charge protocol allows a charging of the cell from 0%SoC to 85%SoC in 26.8 min. To validate the developed charging protocol three cells were cycled with this protocol. Start condition was 25 °C ±1 °C cell temperature and the temperature of the chamber held constant. Cells were cycled in the already presented test setup (refer to Fig. 1) to realize the same test conditions as in second test case. The cycling was started at 0%SoC and the cell was charged with the optimized protocol. Afterwards for relaxation a waiting time of 1 h with following discharge with 1/3 C to 0%SoC has been done. Followed by a further relaxation phase of 2 h. This procedure was repeated for 100 cycles with a capacity check every 25 cycles. After these 100 cycles the state of health (short SoH) of tested cells compared to initial capacity was over 95% and no abnormalities (for example voltage shoulder during relaxation phase) during whole test time occurred. In comparison cycling the cells with same test procedure from 0% to 80% SoC with a constant charging current of 1/3 C at 25 °C for 100 cycles, show a discharge capacity loss of not even 4%, means a SoH of over 96%. During this test about 95% of the Ah throughput for the 100 cycles in comparison to 100 fast charge cycles has been done. Based on the comparison of capacity retention after 100cycles from both tests no abnormal capacity loss based on fast charging could be shown.

2.2. Fast-charging protocol
Because of the internal resistance behavior, the highest charging current 4 C is applied when the cell ' s internal resistance is at the lower values. This approach results in a more energy ef fi cient charging process. The last two stages of the charging process are applied as the cell ' s internal resistance increases rapidly; this procedure helps to decrease the cell ' s temperature to its initial value (see Fig. 2 (d)). The charging current rate at 4 C was selected because it is close to the maximum charging current recommended by the manufacturer (10 A); a security margin of 12% was selected to avoid working at the limiting current, which reduced the likelihood of overheating. The last stage of the fast-charging procedure provides better cell preservation by limiting constant voltage charging to 5 min, thus avoiding an acceleration of the aging process that occurs at high SOC values over longer periods of time [12].

Conclusions
Based on the features of the semi-optimal protocol, two practical novel fast charging protocols were proposed, namely the voltage ramping protocol and the multiple CCCV protocol. The simulation results showed that for the 2.5 mAh cm -2 cell, the maximum capacity after 10 min charge at 30 °C without lithium plating can be improved by up to 10.7% using the proposed protocols compared with the standard CCCV protocol. To achieve 80% charge in 10 min, the proposed protocols will require a charging temperature that is 8 °C lower than that of the CCCV protocol, which minimizes parasitic reactions and prolongs battery life. Finally, we predicted that the proposed protocols are more effective for the fast charging of high loading cells. For a 4 mAh cm -2 cell, the proposed protocols can improve the charge rate by up to 18.8% without lithium plating according to model prediction.
While this work only considered the driving force for lithium plating of a fresh cell as the optimization metric, other degradation mechanisms such as loss of lithium inventory, loss of active materials and increase of cell resistance can be taken into account in a similar manner. Also, these degradation mechanisms may change the lithium plating behavior of the cell, which necessitates adjusting the fast charge protocol as the cell ages. These will be the topics of our future work. Finally, results reported in this article are based on simulation only. Experimental validation of the proposed fast charging protocols is ongoing to verify their improved extreme fast charging capability and cycle life over traditional protocols.

5. Conclusion
This work proposes a fast charging protocol optimization method for lithium ion batteries based on the dynamic programming optimization technique and the physics-based electrochemical-thermal-capacity fade coupled  model.  The  optimization  goal  is  to  determine  the  charging current  profile  as  a  function  of  the  SOC  (charging  stage)  and  the charging-discharging  cycle  for  a  four-stage  charging  protocol  with 15 min charging time and 20% -80% cycling SOC range. The optimiza­ tion  considers  various cost functions including reducing the capacity fade due to the SEI increase, increasing the SEI potential to avoid lithium plating,  and  decreasing  the  temperature  rise  to  prevent  thermal runaway. Comparing with the constant current charging, the proposed multi-stage charge protocol can reduce the capacity fade ratio by 4.6% after  3300  charging-discharging  cycles.
